Ladies and Gentlemen,
Thank you for the opportunity to provide my input on the proposed changes to the
landscape point requirements of the City of Cheyenne Unified Development Code. I feel
strongly that the proposed changes are misguided andwill not benefit the City or local
developers in any significant way.
Iam a licensed landscape architect in the State of Wyoming and am currently self-
employed as a landscape architectural consultant.I hold a BS in Landscape Horticulture with an
emphasis in Landscape Design and Contracting from Colorado State University as well as an
MLA, Master of Landscape Architecture from the University of Colorado, Denver.I have been
designing, building and maintaining landscapes for more than 20 years.I considered myself a
rather reluctant regulator while working as a Planner for the City of Cheyenne Development
Office from2008 to2012 but, after4years with the CityI came to understand that without some
reasonable regulations, many developers would not consider mitigating the impacts of their
developments if it were not for City requirements.
I understand that people are frustrated by the new code and want to see changes. I hope
they arewilling to consider all its subtle nuisances rather than demanding change simply for
change's sake.I believe that simply reducing the landscape point requirement is a much too
simplistic resolution to the various changes that are incorporated into the U.D.C.Iam confused
that we are goinghere, given the implementation of a Unified Development Code that hasfar
greater impacts for development such as architectural requirements that regulate the design and

which requires that even the smallest of proposed building additions or possibly even

only landscaping but also upgrades to all aspects of their site such as decorative fencing,

One item that has changed, and is likely complicating the unchanged landscape point
the MUB and NB districts.One project Irecently worked on in the MUB District would have

Under the U.D.C., my client was required to provide 12.6 points of internal landscaping for the

further directing the placement of the landscape points.This, along with regulating architectural
and other design aesthetics, maybe a problem with the code.

Landscape Code History in Cheyenne
·1992 - The first adopted a landscape code in 1992.
·1999-Laramie County adopted the same landscape code
·2002-The City and County both required automatic irrigation for most new landscaping
·2005-The City added a cash-in-lieu requirement for administrative or variance
reductions in trees to be used by the City to install trees in the City.
·2007-The current regulations took effect.This includes utilizing a point system which
reduced the internal tree requirement by approximately 20%, reduced the street tree
requirement byup to 50% and created more water wise options and a more predictable
framework.
·2012-UDC adopted.The UDC carried forward the majority of the landscape
requirements and included reductions in landscape requirements for more compact
development in the NB, MUB and MUR zone districts and additional flexibility for
existing sites and added a plant material requirement of zoning buffers.
Current Landscape Code Overview
The landscape requirement applies across all zone districts. Landscape evaluation is triggered
when a site planis required.A site is triggered for new development and changes ofuse or
building additions. In cases where there is a building addition the landscape requirements are
system. The points required vary between zone districts based on the maximum coverage
allowed in a district.The points are derived based on the amount of property not allowed to be
covered by buildings and parking lots.Forexample the Community Business district(CB)has a
maximum coverage of 85%, thus the landscape points are computed based on 15% of the
property. By comparison the Central Business District (CBD) downtown has a maximum
coverage of 100% thus no landscape points are required.
The landscape points have been calibrated over time to allow the points tobe functionally
distributed across various landscape components. The primary landscape components include
the landscape setback, parking lots, buffers, foundation plantings and the remainder of the site.
They also addresshow“coverage”of non-tree and non-grass landscaping determined.
A landscape setback is arequired landscape area between the street right of way and parking lot.
This element of landscaping helps to transition the public areas along the street into the areas on
the property. The landscape setback buffers the pedestrians on the sidewalk from the vehicular
area within the site and establishes queuing areasfor vehicles entering and leaving the site.The
setback is often used to helpmanage and clean storm water runoff before it enters the public
storm sewers. The setback also provides aesthetic buffers from the street to parking areas.

Past Landscape Code Revisions
The landscape regulations were substantially updated in 2007.The update in 2007revised the
landscape codeto address flexibility, concerns about quantities and provided water wise options
and encouragements.The framework for the code was altered in 2007 toinclude the point
system which makes it easier to incorporate a widerrange of options and to do so in a predictable
framework.The update also incorporated significant quantity reductions, reducing internal trees
by up to 20% and street trees by up to 50%.It also provided opportunities for significant
toward the landscape requirement and weighted the points infavor of morewater wise
landscaping species.
TheUDC carried this regulation forward with minor adjustments to the maximum coverage of
the Neighborhood Business zone districts (NB) whichin most cases increased the maximum
UDC updated the parking lot standards to reduce the landscape standards for smaller parking lots
and parking lots located to therear and sides of buildings in an effort to encourage development
and redevelopment of smaller more compacts lots. The standards were also modified to allow
for more flexible design of parking lot landscaping.TheUDC also looked to facilitate additional
building reuse by“grandfathering” the parking lot design of existing parking lots.The UDC
clarified requirements for when foundation plantings arerequired and clarified planting
requirements for zoning buffers.These changes made no net increase in the point requirement.
The other major changewith the U DC regarding the landscaping code was adding the ability to
address redevelopment in a more flexible way by authorizing landscaping improvements
associated with building expansions to be proportionate with the expansion and the addition of
administrative adjustments which provides additional flexibility for existing sites.The
administrative adjustment provision applies to landscaping as well as other design standards.

Variance/Relief Requests
An avenue forrelief of the landscape requirement is the variance process. This process allows
the applicant to seek relief from a particular design standard by way of review and determination
of the Board of Adjustment, whichis a sevenmember board.One measurement of the
appropriateness of a particular regulation is to look at the number of times relief is sought from
the requirement.When thereis a consistent request for relief from a particular requirement then
it maybe an indication that the requirement needs to be reviewed.
After the Landscape code was updated in 2007 over 260 site plans have been processed from
2008 through today.During that same period of time18variances havebeen requested for the
landscape coverage requirement or about 7% of projects. Since the UDC was adopted there have
been no requestsfor a variance from the internal landscape requirement.The expectation was
therewould be fewer variance requests with the U DC with the additional flexibility in the code
aimed at infill and building reuse proposals. Thus far the changes in the UDC appear to have
improved the situation with no variance requests for any of onsite landscape requirements
through60site projects submitted todate.

Proposal
The proposal is to reduce the landscape point requirement in half across all developments and to
reduce coverage requirement of the remaining points by a third from 75% to 50%. This will
impact all new developments and redevelopment projects.
Staff received the ordinance from Councilman Shan or via email on June26,2013with
instructions to place the item on the Planning Commission agenda for July 15, 2013.
Councilman Shanor was informed that this was not enough time for legal advertisement and
ordinanceis also sponsored by Councilmen Cook and Allen.
A legal advertisement was place in the newspaper to advertise the public hearing.Planning
Commission will need to act on this item which mayinclude recommendations to approved,
deny, amend or postpone to a meeting occurring within 60 days.

reducing thecost of development and maintenance by the landowners.
